screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will move from the hazards of manual new and delete to a reliable, idiomatic C++ solution: smart pointers following RAII. You will learn why tying resource lifetime to object lifetime reduces leaks and dangling pointers, and how std::unique_ptr enforces a single owner for dynamic memory. Each concept will be grounded with compact code examples and a hands-on refactor pattern you can apply right away. By the end you'll be able to pick unique_ptr when a single owner is required and refactor raw pointer code into safer, clearer ownership. As you explore the slides, notice the concrete examples and the short refactor exercise at the end — try to map a raw pointer in your own code to one of the patterns here. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Intro to unique_ptr
Introduction to std::unique_ptr
Why RAII and exclusive ownership reduce runtime errors in C++ programs.

Smart pointers are thin wrapper objects that manage raw pointers' lifetime. std::unique_ptr enforces a single owner and calls the appropriate delete when it is destroyed, so memory is released deterministically. Use make_unique to construct safely and prefer move for transfers.

Problem
Risks
Solution
Explore Key Topics
In this lesson you'll find code-first examples, ownership patterns, and a small refactor activity to replace raw new/delete.
RAII
Automatic cleanup
Unique
Exclusive ownership
Move
Transfer safely
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Ownership sketch
Raw pointer: manual delete required.
unique_ptr: destructor frees memory reliably.
Quick example
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>

auto p = std::make_unique<int>(42); // owned and freed automatically
Key Takeaway

Prefer std::unique_ptr for single-owner dynamic objects. It makes ownership explicit and destruction deterministic.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next slides you'll develop a practical skill set for managing dynamic memory with std::unique_ptr. First, you'll learn RAII: the pattern that ties resource acquisition to object lifetime so resources are cleaned even during exceptions. Second, you'll learn why raw pointers with explicit new and delete lead to leaks, double deletes, and dangling pointers. Third, you'll become comfortable declaring and initializing std::unique_ptr for single objects and arrays using the make_unique helper. Fourth, you'll see how unique_ptr enforces exclusive ownership: the compiler prevents accidental copies. Each of these objectives trains you to reason about ownership explicitly. For example, by preferring make_unique you avoid mismatched new/delete and improve exception safety. By the end of this first objectives screen you'll be able to explain RAII, list the common perils of manual memory, and write a basic unique_ptr that constructs and destroys an object automatically. Practice identifying one allocation in your code that would benefit from this pattern.

screens.title: Manual new/delete: risks and runtime surprises
screens.narratorSegment: Start by confronting the root problem: manual memory management. When you allocate with new and must remember to call delete, ownership is implicit and fragile. A typical mistake is forgetting delete on every early return path, which causes memory leaks. Another is deleting a pointer twice when ownership is transferred but not cleared, leading to undefined behavior and possible program crashes. Dangling pointers occur when an object is deleted but references to it remain, so subsequent use leads to unpredictable behavior. Concretely, imagine a function that allocates a buffer and, on an error path, returns without freeing it; over time this leaks memory. Or consider two parts of code both assuming they own a pointer and both call delete; that double free is catastrophic. The safer approach binds acquisition and release to the same object, so the destructor cleans up automatically. This contrast matters because many bugs only appear in long runs or under exception conditions. A good mental model is ownership clarity: either one clear owner, or a controlled shared mechanism with explicit policies. In the next slides we'll see the exact mechanism that enforces that clarity.

keyIdea.title: Problem
keyIdea.text: Raw new/delete creates implicit ownership and fragile lifetimes that cause leaks, double frees, and dangling pointers.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Manual new/delete
Comparison
Raw pointers vs RAII-managed
Raw pointer: allocation uses new; programmer must delete on every exit path. Risk: leaks and double deletes.
RAII-managed: constructor acquires, destructor releases automatically, safe across exceptions and returns.
Concrete scenario
A function allocates a buffer, then encounters an error and returns early. If delete was not called, memory leaks. If another code path also deletes the same pointer, double free occurs.
// risky pattern
int* buf = new int[100];
if (error) return; // leaked if delete not called
Misconception
Some think manual control is always faster. In practice, the small wrapper of a smart pointer has negligible overhead while preventing class of bugs that cost much more time to debug.
Try this thought

Find a function in your code that performs dynamic allocation and imagine who must call delete on every path. If it's more than one place, it's a bug waiting to happen.

Key Takeaway

Implicit ownership leads to bugs. Make ownership explicit and predictable to avoid runtime surprises.

screens.title: RAII — the organizing idiom
screens.narratorSegment: RAII stands for Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. The core claim is simple: acquire a resource in a constructor and release it in the destructor, so the object's lifetime determines the resource lifetime. This guarantees cleanup on normal returns, early returns, and exceptions because destructors run automatically when an object goes out of scope. For dynamic memory, smart pointers are RAII wrappers: the pointer object holds the raw pointer and calls delete in its destructor. A concrete example is a wrapper that opens a file in its constructor and closes it in the destructor; you never need to remember a matching close in every error path. A common misconception is that RAII complicates exceptions; in reality it simplifies exception safety by centralizing cleanup logic. When converting legacy code, focus on local temporaries and members that currently call delete manually. Replace them with a RAII object so you get deterministic destruction. As a learner, try to verbalize what owns each resource in one of your functions. If ownership is unclear, RAII is the right pattern to apply. RAII — the organizing idiom means tie acquisition to construction and release to destruction so cleanup is automatic and exception-safe.. In practical terms, how tying resources to object lifetime guarantees cleanup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: RAII recap
keyIdea.text: Tie acquisition to construction and release to destruction so cleanup is automatic and exception-safe.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › RAII
RAII — Resource Acquisition Is Initialization
Bind resource lifetime to object lifetime so destruction is automatic.
Definition: Acquire in constructor, release in destructor. Works uniformly for memory, files, locks, and sockets.
Benefit: deterministic cleanup, exception safety, and centralized resource management.
Misconception: RAII is only for memory. In fact, it applies to any resource needing deterministic release.
Analogy
Think of RAII as borrowing a library book: you check it out at the desk and it is automatically checked back in when you drop it in the return box. The object ensures the return happens.
Concrete example
class FileHandle {
public:
  FileHandle(const char* path) { /* open file */ }
  ~FileHandle(){ /* close file */ }
};
// File closed automatically when FileHandle is destroyed
Key Takeaway

Use RAII to centralize cleanup logic. Smart pointers are a direct RAII application for dynamic memory.

screens.title: What is a smart pointer?
screens.narratorSegment: A smart pointer is a small class wrapper that behaves like a pointer but adds automatic resource management. The wrapper holds a raw pointer internally and implements a destructor that releases the resource, usually by calling delete or delete array. Because the wrapper is an object, its destructor runs when it goes out of scope, which is the RAII pattern in action. Smart pointers also define pointer-like operators so you can use the arrow and dereference operators as usual. The important semantic difference is ownership: smart pointer types encode ownership policies. unique_ptr is exclusive owner; shared_ptr uses reference counting; weak_ptr observes without owning. In this chapter we focus on unique_ptr. A concrete example is replacing a raw pointer member with a unique_ptr member: this makes the owning class responsible for cleanup without writing a destructor. A common mistake is exposing the raw pointer via get() and then letting it be deleted elsewhere — that breaks ownership. Prefer transferring ownership with move when handing the resource to another scope. Reflect: when you see a naked raw pointer, ask who is responsible for delete. If the answer is unclear, wrap it in a smart pointer.

keyIdea.title: Smart pointer
keyIdea.text: A class wrapper that provides pointer semantics and automatic cleanup through RAII.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Smart pointer
Smart Pointer — definition and behavior
Acts like a pointer while owning and managing the lifetime of a resource automatically.
Mechanism: wrapper holds raw pointer and calls delete in its destructor.
Operators: supports arrow and dereference so usage remains familiar.
Ownership: the type encodes ownership policy — unique, shared, or weak.
Quick rule
If no two components should delete the same resource, use unique_ptr. If multiple owners must coexist, consider shared_ptr instead.
Concrete refactor
// before
Foo* f = new Foo();
// ...
delete f;

// after
auto f = std::make_unique<Foo>(); // destroyed automatically
Key Takeaway

Smart pointers preserve pointer syntax while giving deterministic cleanup. unique_ptr is the single-owner form.

screens.title: Creating and using std::unique_ptr
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a canonical pattern for constructing and using unique pointers. The recommended way is to use the make_unique helper; it avoids explicit new and is safer in the presence of exceptions. Once you have a unique_ptr, you use the normal pointer operations to call methods or access members. For example, constructing a resource via make_unique ties creation to ownership immediately. A common concrete example is creating a file handle or a resource object and then calling one of its methods. If you need to check whether the unique pointer is empty, you can compare it to nullptr. A frequent misconception is that unique_ptr imposes heavy overhead; in practice it is a tiny wrapper with negligible cost compared to the benefit of automatic destruction. When you need to access the raw pointer to interact with C APIs, use get(), but do so carefully: the unique_ptr still owns the resource and will free it at destruction. Always avoid manually deleting a raw pointer returned by get. This pattern keeps your code readable and exception-safe while clarifying ownership. Creating and using std::unique_ptr means use std::make_unique to create objects, then use pointer-like operations. check for nullptr to test ownership.. In practical terms, prefer make_unique; use arrow and dereference as usual. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use std::make_unique to create objects, then use pointer-like operations. Check for nullptr to test ownership.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Create & use
Constructing unique_ptr safely
Prefer the make_unique helper to avoid raw new and improve exception safety.
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>

auto r = std::make_unique<MyResource>("FileHandle");
if (r) r->doSomething();
Checking r for truthiness is the usual way to test whether it owns an object. When r goes out of scope, its destructor deletes the owned object.
Caution with get()
get() returns the raw pointer. Use it for interop but do not take ownership or call delete on the returned pointer; unique_ptr still owns it.
Key Takeaway

Construct with make_unique. Use pointer operations naturally and avoid manual delete when unique_ptr owns the resource.

screens.title: Move semantics and transferring ownership
screens.narratorSegment: unique_ptr enforces exclusive ownership by deleting its copy constructor. To transfer ownership you must move the unique pointer. Moving transfers the raw pointer to the destination and leaves the source empty, typically holding nullptr afterward. This behavior is essential when returning dynamically allocated objects from functions or when inserting unique pointers into containers. For example, assigning anotherGadget = std::move(myGadget) transfers ownership, and checking myGadget for null confirms the transfer. A common concrete pattern is returning a unique pointer from a factory function: returning by value performs a move, giving the caller ownership. A misconception is that move implies copying the underlying object; with unique_ptr, move only changes the owner and does not duplicate the resource. When moving into containers, use push_back(std::move(ptr)) so the container takes ownership. After a move, do not dereference the moved-from pointer; treat it as empty. As a practice, refactor a function that previously returned a raw pointer to instead return a unique_ptr by value and observe clear destructor calls. Move semantics and transferring ownership means use std::move to transfer unique_ptr ownership; the source becomes empty and the destination owns the resource.. In practical terms, how std::move changes who owns the resource. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Move semantics
Transfer ownership with move
Moving transfers ownership without copying the resource.
Step 1: Construct a unique_ptr using make_unique.
Step 2: Transfer ownership with std::move(destination = std::move(source)).
Step 3: After move, source becomes null; do not dereference it.
Example: function return
std::unique_ptr<LargeObject> createLargeData() {
  return std::make_unique<LargeObject>(); // moved to caller
}
Common misconception
Moving is not copying. The managed object is not duplicated; only the pointer ownership moves to a new wrapper.
Key Takeaway

Use move semantics when handing ownership across scopes. After the move, treat the source as empty.

screens.title: Passing unique_ptr to functions and receiving it back
screens.narratorSegment: Passing unique_ptr to a function by value transfers ownership to the callee. If the function should not take ownership, pass a raw pointer or a reference to the object instead. When you intend to give ownership to the function, pass by value and use std::move at the call site. For example, processResource(std::move(res)) moves ownership into the function; when the function exits, the resource is destroyed if not moved out again. Returning a unique_ptr by value is the idiomatic factory pattern: the function creates a resource with make_unique and returns it; the caller receives ownership via move semantics. A common example is a createGadget function that returns a unique_ptr to a newly constructed Gadget. A misconception is treating pass-by-value like copy: with unique_ptr it is a transfer. When storing unique_ptrs in containers, moves are required for insertion because copying is forbidden. As a rule of thumb, think about whether the callee should own the resource; if yes, pass a unique_ptr by value; if no, pass a raw pointer or reference and document lifetime expectations. Passing unique_ptr to functions and receiving it back means pass unique_ptr by value to transfer ownership, or return unique_ptr by value from factory functions to hand ownership to the caller.. In practical terms, ownership transfer by value and returning a unique_ptr from factories. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Passing & returning
Pass by value to transfer ownership
Use std::move at the call site to transfer ownership into a function that should take responsibility.
void processResource(std::unique_ptr<MyResource> res) {
  res->doSomething();
} // res destroyed here

// caller
processResource(std::move(resourcePtr));
Factory return pattern
Returning a unique_ptr from a function hands ownership to the caller without copies.
std::unique_ptr<Gadget> createGadget() {
  return std::make_unique<Gadget>("G101");
}
Key Takeaway

Decide who should own a resource before passing. Use move for transfer and prefer returning unique_ptr from factories.

screens.title: unique_ptr with arrays
screens.narratorSegment: unique_ptr supports arrays through a specialized form. When you manage an array, declare unique_ptr with square brackets so it calls delete array when destroyed. This ensures each element's destructor runs and the memory is freed appropriately. A concrete example: std::unique_ptr arr = std::make_unique (3) creates an array of three MyResource objects managed by unique_ptr. You can then access elements with the subscript operator and rely on automatic deletion when arr goes out of scope. Watch out: assigning array elements may use move or copy semantics depending on the type, and make_unique for arrays constructs elements in place. Use the array specialization so delete[] is called at destruction.

screens.title: Storing unique_ptr in containers
screens.narratorSegment: Containers such as std::vector can hold unique_ptrs, but because unique_ptr is not copyable you must move elements into the container. For example, calling push_back(std::make_unique (...)) constructs the unique_ptr in place or moving an existing unique_ptr with push_back(std::move(ptr)). This pattern is useful when you want a collection of objects each owned exclusively by the container. When iterating the container, use references to unique_ptr or access elements with get() if necessary for interop, always respecting ownership semantics. When removing elements, be mindful of who will own the removed resource; you can extract ownership by moving the unique_ptr out before erasing. A common pattern is to store unique_ptrs for polymorphic objects so the container manages lifetimes and the correct destructors run. A pitfall is attempting to copy the container's elements: copying a vector of unique_ptr is a compile-time error. The recommended workflow is explicit move operations and clear documentation of who owns resources at each stage. Practically, storing unique_ptrs makes ownership explicit and centralizes cleanup with the container's lifetime. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring mistakes when developers start using unique_ptr. The first is trying to copy a unique_ptr; the compiler prevents this because copying would imply two owners. If you need shared ownership, choose a different smart pointer type. Second, mixing manual delete with unique_ptr-managed memory leads to double delete; never call delete on a pointer owned by a unique_ptr. Third, careless use of get() exposes the raw pointer and can tempt someone to delete it or store it beyond the owning object's lifetime. When you must pass a raw pointer to an A P I that does not accept ownership, use get() but document that the callee must not delete it. Fourth, returning dangling raw pointers extracted from a unique_ptr without transferring ownership causes use-after-free bugs. A simple rule prevents these mistakes: if you need to transfer ownership, move the unique_ptr; if you need to observe without owning, pass a raw pointer or reference but ensure the owner outlives the observer. Practice: attempt to compile an example where you copy a unique_ptr and observe the compile-time error — that error teaches the rule directly.

You will learn why tying resource lifetime to object lifetime reduces leaks and dangling pointers, and how std::unique_ptr enforces a single owner for dynamic memory. We'll see how to create unique pointers safely with the make_unique helper, how ownership transfers with move semantics, how arrays are managed, and common mistakes to avoid. Each concept will be grounded with compact code examples and a hands-on refactor pattern you can apply right away. This matters because production C++ systems rely on predictable destruction, especially when exceptions or early returns occur. By the end you'll be able to pick unique_ptr when a single owner is required and refactor raw pointer code into safer, clearer ownership. As you explore the slides, notice the concrete examples and the short refactor exercise at the end — try to map a raw pointer in your own code to one of the patterns here. Which allocation in your project could be owned by a unique pointer?

Over the next slides you'll develop a practical skill set for managing dynamic memory with std::unique_ptr. First, you'll learn RAII: the pattern that ties resource acquisition to object lifetime so resources are cleaned even during exceptions. Second, you'll learn why raw pointers with explicit new and delete lead to leaks, double deletes, and dangling pointers. Third, you'll become comfortable declaring and initializing std::unique_ptr for single objects and arrays using the make_unique helper. Fourth, you'll see how unique_ptr enforces exclusive ownership: the compiler prevents accidental copies. Each of these objectives trains you to reason about ownership explicitly. For example, by preferring make_unique you avoid mismatched new/delete and improve exception safety. By the end of this first objectives screen you'll be able to explain RAII, list the common perils of manual memory, and write a basic unique_ptr that constructs and destroys an object automatically. Practice identifying one allocation in your code that would benefit from this pattern.

This second objectives slide focuses on moving from understanding to application. First, you'll practice transferring ownership with move semantics so that a unique pointer can be returned from functions or stored in containers. Second, you'll recognize appropriate use cases for unique_ptr: local temporaries, members that exclusively own resources, and function returns that hand over ownership. Third, you'll learn how to manage dynamic arrays via std::unique_ptr specialized for arrays and why delete[] must match array ownership. Fourth, you'll learn common mistakes such as attempting to copy a unique_ptr, mixing manual delete with unique_ptr ownership, and misusing get() to expose raw pointers without clear lifetime guarantees. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or scenario to help you choose patterns in your code. Practice by refactoring a raw pointer factory function to return a unique pointer.

Start by confronting the root problem: manual memory management. When you allocate with new and must remember to call delete, ownership is implicit and fragile. A typical mistake is forgetting delete on every early return path, which causes memory leaks. RAII stands for Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. There are recurring mistakes when developers start using unique_ptr. The first is trying to copy a unique_ptr; the compiler prevents this because copying would imply two owners. If you need shared ownership, choose a different smart pointer type. Second, mixing manual delete with unique_ptr-managed memory leads to double delete; never call delete on a pointer owned by a unique_ptr. Third, careless use of get() exposes the raw pointer and can tempt someone to delete it or store it beyond the owning object's lifetime. Let's summarize the essential points to remember. First, RAII binds resource lifetime to object lifetime so resources are cleaned deterministically. Second, std::unique_ptr is a smart pointer enforcing exclusive ownership: it cannot be copied and will free its owned object when destroyed. Third, use make_unique to construct unique_ptr instances safely and prefer moves to transfer ownership. Fourth, unique_ptr supports arrays via the array specialization so delete[] is called automatically. Fifth, common mistakes include attempting to copy unique_ptr, mixing manual delete with managed resources, and exposing raw pointers without clear lifetime guarantees. Keep ownership small and explicit.
